<reason>B won the framing fight that decided the debate. A's opening pinned its case to an enforcement/vagueness objection ("who adjudicates 'when'?"), but B correctly showed the motion is addressed to platforms as a normative claim, and that platforms already hold the relevant evidence (A/B tests, holdout cohorts, churn and complaint data). That reframe was legitimate rather than evasive, and it turned A's central objection into a category error. B also landed the sharpest substantive hit of the debate on boosts: sponsored listings do not degrade organic results, whereas attention here is zero-sum, so a boost is literally someone else's suppression, and disclosure to the buyer is not disclosure to the demoted user. A never answered the third-party-consent point, replying only that scarcity is natural. B's parent-company point plus the detectability asymmetry also blunted A's competition mechanism. A did land real damage — the "you cannot have it both ways on detectability" question was answered coherently (aggregate direction, not precise diagnosis, drives exit), and A's point that "degrades outcomes" is a contested tradeoff even with perfect data is genuinely live. But A's direct answer to B's binary — a flat "no obligation" even when a platform's own data shows harm — handed B the cleanest voting reason in the round, and B pressed it hard by noting the motion's word "when" already concedes hard cases and only asks about clear ones. A's closing restated vagueness rather than repairing the concession. B's opening was clipped for length, a modest execution cost, but not enough to offset the comparative advantage.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's pressure question forcing a yes/no on whether a platform whose own holdout data shows a mechanic degrades matches owes any change, followed by A's answer of "no," which B then crystallized as negating the proposition outright and reduced A's vagueness objection to an argument about degree rather than about "nothing."</best_rebuttal>
